Every deployment we've covered so far needs a server running R. Posit Connect Cloud runs R for us (@sec-posit-connect-cloud). Docker packages R into a container (@sec-docker), and GitHub Actions builds and ships it (@sec-gha-cicd). In this chapter we'll remove the server entirely. We'll use webR and shinylive to run our app-package in the user's browser.

```{r}
#| label: shinypak_apps
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
shinypak_apps(regex = "^22", branch = "22_webr")
```

## What is webR? {#sec-webr-what-is-webr}

[webR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) is a version of R that runs in a web browser. It's compiled to [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/), a binary format that modern browsers run at near native speed. When a browser loads webR, the R session lives on the user's machine, not on a server.

[shinylive](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) builds on webR. It packages a Shiny app, webR, and the app's R packages into a folder of static files. A static file host is just a web server that hands out files without running any code (GitHub Pages and Netlify are common examples).

The diagram below compares a server-based deployment with a shinylive deployment:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: 'Server-based Shiny versus shinylive'
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"16px", "darkMode":false}}}%%

flowchart TD
    subgraph Server["<strong>Server-based Shiny</strong>"]
        B1(["Browser"]) <-->|"inputs and outputs"| R1("R process on a server<br>runs <code>launch_app()</code>")
    end
    subgraph Live["<strong>shinylive</strong>"]
        H1["Static file host"] -->|"i. download app files"| B2(["Browser"])
        B2 -->|"ii. start"| W1("webR inside the browser<br>runs the app")
    end

    style Server fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10
    style Live fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10
    style R1 fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style W1 fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
```

In a server-based deployment, every click travels to the server and every plot travels back. In a shinylive deployment, the host only delivers the files. After the first download, the app runs without contacting a server at all.

### Trade-offs

shinylive removes the server, but the browser takes on the server's job. I've found these trade-offs matter most for app-packages:

* First load: the browser downloads webR and every package before the app appears, so the first visit takes longer than a server-based app.

* Visible code: all the app's code and data are sent to the browser. Never put credentials, API keys, or private data in a shinylive app.

* No system tools: webR can't call programs installed on a computer. Features that rely on the Quarto CLI or `system()` calls won't work.

* Temporary files: webR writes files to a virtual file system in browser memory. Log files written with `logger` disappear when the user closes the tab.

## Which packages run in webR? {#sec-webr-packages}

webR can't install packages from source. Every package an app uses needs a precompiled WebAssembly binary. The webR project hosts thousands of these binaries in a CRAN-like repository at <https://repo.r-wasm.org>.

Before we export anything, we should confirm that each package in our `Imports` field has a binary. The code below reads the `DESCRIPTION` file and compares it to the packages in the webR repository:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
wasm_pkgs <- available.packages(
  contriburl = "https://repo.r-wasm.org/bin/emscripten/contrib/4.5"
)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = "base"))
imports <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = "Imports")
imports <- trimws(strsplit(imports, ",")[[1]])
imports <- imports[imports != ""]
setdiff(imports, c(rownames(wasm_pkgs), base_pkgs))
```

Base packages (like `tools`) ship with webR, so we remove them before we compare. An empty result means every dependency has a binary:

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
character(0)
```

:::

The `4.5` in the URL refers to the version of R that webR is built on. Check the [webR documentation](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/packages.html) for the current version if this URL stops working.

## A WebAssembly binary for `sap` {#sec-webr-r-universe}

Our dependencies are covered, but `sap` itself isn't on CRAN, so it has no binary in the webR repository. We need a service that builds one for us. [R-universe](https://r-universe.dev/) is a free service from rOpenSci that builds R packages from GitHub. It builds a WebAssembly binary of every package it hosts.

To set up a personal universe:

1. Create a GitHub repository named `<username>.r-universe.dev` (for this book, `mjfrigaard.r-universe.dev`).

2. Add a `packages.json` file that lists each package and the repository it comes from.

3. Install the [R-universe GitHub app](https://github.com/apps/r-universe/installations/new) on your account.

The `packages.json` file below adds `sap` to the universe. The `branch` field tells R-universe to build from the `22_webr` branch instead of the default branch:

```{verbatim}
[
  {
    "package": "sap",
    "url": "https://github.com/mjfrigaard/sap",
    "branch": "22_webr"
  }
]
```

R-universe rebuilds the package (and its WebAssembly binary) each time we push to that branch. When the build finishes, we install `sap` from the universe instead of from our local source files:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
install.packages(
  "sap",
  repos = c("https://mjfrigaard.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos"))
)
```

### Why install from R-universe?

Installing from R-universe matters because shinylive bundles the packages installed on our machine. The installed package records where it came from, and shinylive uses that record to download the matching WebAssembly binary.

## The shinylive launcher {#sec-webr-launcher}

shinylive exports an app directory (a folder with an `app.R` file), not a package. We'll add a small launcher app in `inst/webr/` that loads `sap` and returns the application:

```{r}
#| label: git_box_22_webr
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
git_margin_box(
  contents = "launch",
  fig_pw = '75%',
  branch = "22_webr",
  repo = 'sap')
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
library(shiny)
library(sap)

shinyApp(
  ui = movies_ui(bslib = TRUE),
  server = movies_server
)
```

This file calls `movies_ui()` and `movies_server()` directly instead of `launch_app()`. `launch_app()` calls `shiny::runApp()`, which starts a server and blocks the R session. shinylive expects `app.R` to return a Shiny app object and handles the rest itself.

The `library(sap)` call also does a second job. shinylive scans `app.R` for `library()` calls to decide which packages to bundle. It finds `sap`, then bundles the binaries for `sap` and each of its dependencies.

## Exporting the app {#sec-webr-export}

We'll store the export code in `dev/webr.R`. The `dev/` folder is already listed in `.Rbuildignore`, so the script won't end up in the built package. `shinylive::export()` converts the launcher into a static site in `_site/`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
shinylive::export(appdir = "inst/webr", destdir = "_site")
```

The export downloads the shinylive assets the first time it runs, so the first export takes a few minutes. Later exports reuse the cached assets.

We can preview the site with `httpuv::runStaticServer()`. Opening `_site/index.html` directly in a browser won't work, because webR needs the files served over HTTP:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
httpuv::runStaticServer("_site")
```

The app should look the same as the version we launch with `launch_app(app = "bslib")`. We can confirm that R is running in the browser by opening the browser's developer tools. The Network tab lists the webR and package files as they download.

We've also added `_site/` to `.gitignore`. The exported site is a build artifact, so we rebuild it from source rather than tracking it in Git.

### Publishing the site

Any static file host can serve the `_site/` folder. GitHub Pages is a common choice. We can build and deploy the site with a workflow like the ones in @sec-gha-cicd. A repository has only one GitHub Pages site, and we'll use the `sap` site for the package website in @sec-pkgdown. If you want both, deploy the shinylive app from a separate repository.

```{r}
#| label: co_box_quarto_live
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "b",
  look = "default", hsize = "1.05", size = "0.95",
  header = "shinylive in Quarto",
  fold = TRUE,
  contents = "
The [`quarto-shinylive` extension](https://github.com/quarto-ext/shinylive) embeds shinylive apps directly in Quarto documents with a `{shinylive-r}` code block. This works well for small examples in documentation, but an app-package with modules and data is easier to maintain as an exported app."
)
```

## Recap {.unnumbered}

webR and shinylive move our app-package from a server into the user's browser. The trade-off is a slower first load and code that's visible to every user.

```{r}
#| label: co_box_recap
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "g",
  fold = FALSE,
  look = "default", hsize = "1.05", size = "0.95",
  header = "Recap",
  contents = "
\n
1. Check that each package in `Imports` has a WebAssembly binary at repo.r-wasm.org.

2. Publish the app-package to R-universe so it gets a WebAssembly binary, then install it from there.

3. Add a launcher `app.R` that returns a Shiny app object instead of calling `runApp()`.

4. Export the launcher with `shinylive::export()` and serve the static files from any web host.")
```

In the next chapter we'll package the same app as a desktop application with `shinyelectron`, which can also use shinylive to run without R installed.
